record.paper_title: Unfolding the Labyrinth: Open Problems in Physics, Mathematics, Astrophysics and Other Areas of Science
record.original_question: Do fundamental constants of nature, especially the gravitational constant G, vary with time or with physical circumstances, and if so what rule governs that variation across celestial-mechanics and terrestrial settings?

evidence.quote: One of interesting questions in recent years is whether the fundamental questions of Nature vary with time?
It gives the changing rule for gravitational coefficient G as follows

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ denote Newton's gravitational constant appearing in the gravitational force law $F = G\,m_1 m_2 / r^2$, and more generally let $\{c_i\}$ denote the dimensionful fundamental constants of nature (such as $G$, the speed of light $c$, Planck's constant $\hbar$, and the fine-structure constant $\alpha$). Determine whether any of these constants—and in particular $G$—are truly invariant, or whether they depend on cosmic time $t$ and/or on the local physical environment (matter density, gravitational potential, scale, etc.). Specifically:

(a) Decide whether $\dot G/G \neq 0$, and if so, give a quantitative law $G = G(t,\mathbf{x};\text{environment})$ governing the variation.

(b) Determine whether the same law (or any consistent law) reconciles the value of $G$ inferred from celestial-mechanical observations (planetary ephemerides, binary pulsar timing, lunar laser ranging, gravitational-wave inspirals of compact binaries, cosmological probes such as the CMB, BAO, and BBN) with the value measured in terrestrial laboratory (Cavendish-type) experiments.

(c) If a variation exists, derive the functional form of $G(t)$ from first principles within a self-consistent theory of gravity and verify its compatibility with the current observational bounds.
artifact.status_search_result: Current observational and laboratory studies through 2025 continue only to place tighter upper bounds on $\dot G/G$ (e.g., $\dot G/G = (0.016 \pm 0.098)\times 10^{-15}\,\text{yr}^{-1}$ from white-dwarf H$_2$ spectra in 2025; cosmological CMB+BAO+BBN measurements in 2025 consistent with the laboratory value within $1\sigma$; gravitational-wave bounds from GW170817 of order $10^{-8}\,\text{yr}^{-1}$). No definitive detection of temporal variation has been established, and no universally accepted law for the variation exists. The problem is therefore open.

status_evidence.title: Searching for cosmic-time variation in the gravitational constant with strongest H2 Werner transitions
status_evidence.snippet: Constraint Ġ/G = (0.016 ± 0.098) × 10^-15 yr^-1 from white-dwarf spectroscopy (2025).
status_evidence.claim: Only upper bounds, no detected variation.

status_evidence.title: Cosmological measurement of the gravitational constant G using the CMB, BAO, and BBN
status_evidence.snippet: G = (6.75 ± 0.12)×10^-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2, compatible with laboratory value within 1σ.
status_evidence.claim: Cosmological and laboratory values currently compatible; no required variation.

status_evidence.title: Constraints on the Time Variation of G from Binary Neutron Star GW Observations
